section.title: Those Who Trust in the Lord
section.sectionRationale: A Song of Ascents, sixth in the pilgrim collection Psalms 120 to 134, placed in Book V of the Psalter, Psalms 107 to 150. Just as Mount Zion's surrounding hills form a natural wall around Jerusalem, this psalm pictures the LORD Himself surrounding His trusting people with unshakeable protection.
section.thesis: Those who trust in the LORD are as immovable as Mount Zion, kept secure by His surrounding presence and His just limits on the reign of the wicked, a security and righteousness fulfilled in Christ who holds His people fast and will never let them be snatched away.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the immovable security of those who trust the LORD, verses 1 to 2, the limit set on the scepter of the wicked, verse 3, and the closing prayer for the righteous and a blessing of peace, verses 4 to 5.

verses.text: Those who {{batach|trust}} in the LORD are like Mount Zion. It cannot be moved; it abides forever.
As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds His people, both now and forevermore.
For the scepter of the wicked will not rest upon the land allotted to the righteous, so that the righteous will not put forth their hands to injustice.
Do good, O LORD, to those who are good, and to the upright in heart.
But those who turn to crooked ways the LORD will banish with the evildoers. Peace be upon Israel.

batach.gloss: To trust, feel secure, rely confidently on someone; here the ground of an unshakeable stability, like Mount Zion itself, given to those who trust the LORD.

basic.context: This Song of Ascents pictures Jerusalem's surrounding hills as a portrait of the LORD's protection of His trusting people, and prays that His just rule, not the scepter of the wicked, would govern the land allotted to the righteous.
basic.hermeneutics: It describes Israel's confidence in the LORD's protection and just governance over her land, and it prescribes as an abiding pattern trusting the LORD as an unshakeable foundation and praying for His people's uprightness and peace.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm opens with batach, trust, the confident reliance that grounds the whole picture of Mount Zion's immovable stability, and closes with shalom, peace, upon Israel, echoing Psalm 122's prayer.
basic.typology: Mount Zion's immovable stability anticipates the security believers have in Christ, who holds His own so that none can snatch them from His hand, and the limited scepter of the wicked anticipates the final judgment when every unrighteous rule gives way to Christ's eternal reign.
basic.christ: Jesus promises that no one will snatch His sheep out of His hand, John 10:28-29, the fulfillment of the security this psalm pictures in Mount Zion, and He is the one whose righteous scepter will finally and fully displace every wicked reign, Hebrews 1:8.
basic.god: The LORD surrounds His trusting people the way mountains ring Jerusalem, guarding them now and forever, and He sets a just limit on the rule of the wicked so that His righteous ones are not driven to injustice by prolonged oppression.
basic.crossReferences: John 10:28-29 shows Christ holding His people fast so none can snatch them away. Matthew 7:24-25 pictures the house built on the rock, unmoved by storm, as this psalm pictures Zion. Hebrews 1:8 sets Christ's righteous scepter over every fading reign of wickedness.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's picture of unshakeable trust and a limited scepter of wickedness is fulfilled in Christ, who holds His people utterly secure and whose righteous, eternal reign will finally displace every unjust power.

context.literary:
Psalm 125 is built like a fortress. Verse 1 lays a foundation, trusting people are like a mountain that cannot move. Verse 2 draws a ring round it, as the mountains stand round Jerusalem, so the LORD stands round His people. Verse 3 sets a limit on what can come inside the ring, and verses 4 and 5 ask for the right sorting of the people within it, the good on one side and the crooked on the other. The poem closes with a blessing, 'Peace be upon Israel,' which acts as a gate.

The key to the structure is the word 'around,' which occurs twice in verse 2. The mountains are round Jerusalem, and the LORD is round His people. The first is a simile, and the second is the thing it describes. The psalm is moving from a picture the pilgrims could see on the horizon to a fact they could not see, and it does so by repeating a word. Verse 2 also holds time in its grip, 'both now and forevermore,' which echoes the 'forever' of verse 1. The security is spatial and temporal. It surrounds and it lasts.

Verse 3 changes the voice from comfort to a reason: 'For the scepter of the wicked will not rest.' It then adds a purpose clause that is unusual, 'so that the righteous will not put forth their hands to injustice.' The point is not only that the LORD protects the righteous from wicked rulers. It is that He protects the righteous from becoming wicked under the pressure of such rule. The psalm is concerned for the soul of the people as well as for their safety.

The last two verses divide the congregation by a prayer, 'Do good, O LORD, to those who are good,' verse 4, and a warning, 'those who turn to crooked ways,' verse 5. A prayer for the faithful and a warning for the faithless stand side by side and close with the benediction. Taken with Psalm 128:6, which ends with the same words, 'Peace be upon Israel,' the Songs of Ascents show that this phrase works like an amen.
context.historical:
Jerusalem sits on a ridge ringed by higher hills. To the east the Mount of Olives rises across the Kidron Valley, and to the north and west other heights close in. A pilgrim walking up from Jericho or from the coastal plain would see the city nestled among them. Verse 2 uses that landscape as a picture: the hills are the city's natural walls. The comparison tells us that the psalm was composed in or near Jerusalem, by people who knew the view.

The 'land allotted to the righteous' refers to the division of Canaan among the tribes, which was done by lot, Joshua 18:6. The word for lot, goral, ties the land to the LORD's own assignment. To say that the wicked's scepter will not 'rest' on that land is to say that foreign or unjust rule should not settle permanently on what God gave. Israel's history shows how real the danger was. After the exile Nehemiah's generation confessed, 'here we are today as slaves in the land You gave our fathers,' and that the harvest went 'to the kings You have set over us because of our sins,' Nehemiah 9:36 to 37. The psalm may arise from just such a season, when a foreign scepter lay over the land and there was a temptation to cooperate with it, to compromise and to take part in its injustice.

That temptation explains the odd phrase of verse 3, 'so that the righteous will not put forth their hands to injustice.' Under long oppression, ordinary people are pressed to bribe, to inform, to cheat, or to take up arms in despair. The psalm prays that the pressure be limited so that the people of God are not broken into wrongdoing. It names the wicked rule and the individual who bends to it, and places both under the LORD's judgment.

The heading of the psalm is only 'A Song of Ascents.' No author is named, so any attempt to fix a date from the text is an inference. The psalm's confidence that Zion 'cannot be moved' was also open to abuse. Jeremiah warned people against chanting, 'This is the temple of the LORD,' as though the building guaranteed safety, Jeremiah 7:4, and Micah said that Zion would be 'plowed like a field,' Micah 3:12, when its leaders were corrupt.
context.canonical:
Psalm 125 draws on the Psalter's theology of Zion. 'God is within her; she will not be moved,' says Psalm 46:5, with the same verb for being moved. The verb appears in the Psalter's portrait of the person who trusts: he who does right 'will never be shaken,' Psalm 15:5, and 'the righteous man will be remembered forever,' Psalm 112:6. Psalm 125 gathers these together and makes the trusting person himself like Mount Zion. The idea that God surrounds His people has a parallel in Psalm 34:7, 'The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him,' and in Zechariah 2:5, where the LORD says, 'I will be a wall of fire around it, and I will be the glory within it.' Elisha's servant saw the same truth when his eyes were opened and he saw that 'the hills were full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha,' 2 Kings 6:17.

The verse about the scepter has a long background. 'The scepter will not depart from Judah,' says Genesis 49:10, until the one to whom it belongs comes. The scepter of the wicked is a rival to the scepter of Judah, and the psalm asks that the right scepter be the one that holds. Psalm 45:6 says of the king, 'justice is the scepter of Your kingdom,' and Hebrews 1:8 applies that line to the Son. Revelation 2:27 and 19:15 speak of the Messiah ruling the nations with an iron scepter.

The New Testament picks up the phrase that closes the psalm. 'Peace and mercy to all who walk by this rule, even to the Israel of God,' says Galatians 6:16, a sentence that echoes 'Peace be upon Israel' and redefines who belongs. In Isaiah 28:16 God lays 'a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation' in Zion, and 'the one who believes will never be shaken.' Hebrews 12:28 says 'we are receiving an unshakable kingdom.' Isaiah 54:10 states the strongest form of the thought, that even if the mountains are removed, 'My loving devotion will not depart from you.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm was written to give a worried people a better thing to look at than their circumstances. Under pressure, people look at the strength of the oppressor, at their own weakness, or at the prospects of compromise. The singer asks them to look at a mountain. The point of the comparison is not that Zion is strong in itself but that those who trust in the LORD share in its steadiness. The stability comes from where the trust is placed.

He also meant them to be reassured about the limits of evil. The wicked have a scepter, and the psalm does not deny it. It says the scepter will not rest on the allotted land. This is a claim about God's government: the LORD keeps a boundary round what the wicked can do and how long they can do it. For people living through a long oppression, that is a message of hope with an edge. The author does not promise that the wicked will have no power, only that their power is bounded.

Finally, the psalm warns Israel about itself. The prayer that the righteous will not turn to injustice recognises that oppression tempts the oppressed. The closing verses separate the upright from those who turn to crooked ways, and that includes people within Israel. The psalm intends the pilgrims to hear the blessing of 'Peace be upon Israel' as something they must be part of by remaining straight, not by descent alone. It is a song of comfort, and it is also a call to integrity.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes God's protection of Zion and His people, and a limit on wicked rule. It does not say that believers will never suffer injustice. The righteous in Israel's history were exiled, killed and oppressed, and Paul quotes Scripture to say that believers face death all day long and are considered as sheep to be slaughtered, Romans 8:36. The psalm's claim is therefore not that trouble is impossible but that the LORD's hold on His people is secure and that evil's reach is bounded.

Its clearest prescription concerns the heart. The prayer is that the righteous will not 'put forth their hands to injustice.' Believers who live under pressure, whether at work, in a society that rewards corruption, or under unjust authorities, may pray the same prayer and take it as a command to resist the pull to compromise. The verse about crooked paths warns every reader to check the direction in which he is walking. The psalm does not tell the church to expect that the wicked will hold no office, nor to demand it, but it does teach that God judges and that leaders and citizens alike answer to Him.

The benediction, 'Peace be upon Israel,' needs care. Paul extends the language to 'the Israel of God,' Galatians 6:16, and says that 'not all who are descended from Israel are Israel,' Romans 9:6. The text asks the reader to see that the people the peace is promised to are the upright in heart, and the New Testament identifies them as all who are in Christ.

debates.question: Does 'the scepter of the wicked' in verse 3 refer to a specific foreign occupier or to wicked rule in general?

views.label: A specific historical oppressor
views.case: The concrete language of a scepter resting on allotted land fits a particular season of foreign or unjust domination over Israel's territory.

views.label: A general principle about wicked rule
views.case: The psalm gives no names or dates, suggesting a broader principle: God limits how long unjust power may weigh on His people, whoever the oppressor.

debates.bearing: Either reading affirms the same pastoral comfort, that God sets real limits on injustice and will not let it permanently corrupt His righteous people.

debates.question: Does the promise that the wicked scepter 'will not rest' on the land conflict with the exile?

views.label: The promise was conditional, and Israel forfeited it
views.case: Jeremiah warned against trusting 'the temple of the LORD' as a charm, Jeremiah 7:4, and Micah said Zion would be plowed like a field because of her leaders, Micah 3:11 to 12. On this reading the psalm's confidence belongs to those who truly trust and are upright, and the nation as a whole lost its protection when it turned away.

views.label: The promise is about limits, not exemption
views.case: The verb means to settle or remain. The psalm does not say the wicked will never touch the land, only that their rule will not settle permanently. The exile ended, and Nehemiah's generation returned, which fits the claim that evil rule has a limit. On this reading the promise held even through the exile.

debates.bearing: The two views agree that the psalm is no guarantee of political safety for a people who ignore God, and that the LORD does set a boundary on evil. The final fulfilment lies in Christ's kingdom, where no wicked scepter will ever come.

debates.question: Who are 'those who turn to crooked ways' in verse 5?

views.label: Apostates inside Israel
views.case: The verb 'turn aside' implies leaving a path one was on, and the phrase appears in a psalm about the people of God. The warning would be against Israelites who yielded to the oppressors' ways and joined their injustice.

views.label: The wicked rulers and their agents
views.case: The verse says the LORD will banish them 'with the evildoers,' who may be the wicked of verse 3. On this reading the psalm closes by returning to the enemies whose scepter was mentioned earlier.

debates.bearing: Either way the psalm teaches that the line between the upright and the crooked does not run along ethnic boundaries alone, and that every reader must ask which path he is on. The blessing at the end is for Israel as the faithful people.

study.originalLanguages:
The opening participle habotchim, 'those who trust,' describes a settled habit and not a single act. The root batach pictures leaning one's weight on something, and the Old Testament sets it against trust in human strength, as in Jeremiah 17:7 to 8, where the one who trusts in the LORD is like a tree planted by water. Isaiah 26:3 to 4 adds that the person who trusts is kept in perfect peace because 'GOD the LORD is the Rock eternal.' In Psalm 125 the person who leans is compared not to a tree but to a mountain, and the grammar of verse 1 leaves a pleasing ambiguity. The clause 'it cannot be moved; it abides forever' can describe Zion, and it can equally describe the person. The verb for 'abides,' yeshev, is the ordinary verb to sit or dwell, and it is used of a person dwelling in a place. The verb 'cannot be moved,' lo yimmot, uses the root mot, 'to totter,' the same root as Psalm 15:5, 'will never be shaken,' and Psalm 46:5, 'she will not be moved.'

The word 'around,' saviv, appears twice in verse 2, once for the mountains and once for the LORD. It is the word for something that encircles on every side, as in Job 1:10, where Satan complains that the LORD has placed 'a hedge on every side around' Job. The phrase 'both now and forevermore' is me'attah ve'ad olam, literally 'from now and until forever.' It is also the closing promise of Psalm 121:8, so that the two psalms, one about the LORD as keeper and one about the LORD as a ring, end on the same note.

Verse 3 turns on the word shevet, 'scepter,' which also means rod, staff and tribe. The tribes of Psalm 122:4 are shivte, the plural of the same word. The wordplay is probably deliberate in a collection where the pilgrims move from the tribes of the LORD to the rod of the wicked. The verb 'rest,' lo yanuach, is the verb that describes the ark coming to rest on the mountains of Ararat, Genesis 8:4. A scepter that does not 'rest' on the land is one that cannot settle in as if it belonged there. The word for the land 'allotted' is goral, 'lot,' the term for the lots cast to divide Canaan, Joshua 18:6. The purpose clause says the righteous will not 'put forth their hands,' shalach yad, 'to send out the hand,' a phrase for reaching out to do something, here to injustice, avlah, which means crookedness or wrong.

Verse 4 has a Hebrew imperative hativah, 'do good,' from the root yatav, and the people who are the object are tovim, 'good ones,' and 'upright in heart,' yishrei lev. The psalm answers the word tov with tov. Psalm 122:9 had closed with 'I will seek your good,' and the pilgrim's seeking is met here by the LORD's own doing of good.

In verse 5 the crooked ways are aqalqalotam, a word that means twisting or winding. It occurs in Judges 5:6, where in days of oppression the travellers 'took the byways,' the twisting paths. The verb for the LORD's action is yolikhem, a causative form of halakh, 'to walk,' so that the LORD 'causes them to walk' away with the evildoers. They have chosen a path and they are led along it to its end. The last line, shalom al Yisrael, 'Peace upon Israel,' ends Psalm 128 as well.

typology.type: Mount Zion that cannot be moved, Psalm 125:1
typology.fulfillment: The trusting are likened to the mountain that cannot be moved. God lays 'a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation' in Zion, and 'the one who believes will never be shaken,' Isaiah 28:16. Peter applies the cornerstone to Christ, and believers who come to Him are 'like living stones,' 1 Peter 2:5. Jesus tells of a house built on the rock that is not shaken by rain and flood, Matthew 7:24 to 25, and promises that 'the gates of Hades will not prevail' against His church, Matthew 16:18. The correspondence is that the stability rests on a foundation God has laid. The type falls short because the earthly Zion was in fact taken and burned, and only the Zion where the Lamb stands, Revelation 14:1, cannot be moved.

typology.type: The LORD surrounding His people, Psalm 125:2
typology.fulfillment: The LORD says of Jerusalem, 'I will be a wall of fire around it, and I will be the glory within it,' Zechariah 2:5. The picture finds a fuller form in Christ who holds His people. 'No one can snatch them out of My hand,' and 'No one can snatch them out of My Father's hand,' John 10:28 to 29, which describes a double ring, the hand of the Son and the hand of the Father. Paul concludes that nothing in all creation 'will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord,' Romans 8:39. The type falls short in that the mountains are inanimate, and the LORD's protection is personal and active.

The psalm sets the scepter of the wicked against the LORD's own rule. Genesis 49:10 promises that the scepter will not depart from Judah until the one to whom it belongs comes. Psalm 45:6 says that 'justice is the scepter of Your kingdom,' and Hebrews 1:8 applies this to the Son. Revelation 19:15 pictures Christ ruling the nations 'with an iron scepter.' The correspondence is the contest between two kinds of rule. In Christ the wicked scepter is replaced by a righteous one that does not rest on the land for a season but is established for ever. The type falls short because the psalm only asks for a limit, while Christ brings the end.

typology.type: The land allotted to the righteous, Psalm 125:3
typology.fulfillment: The land given by lot to the tribes is a sign of an inheritance. Jesus says, 'Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth,' Matthew 5:5, echoing Psalm 37:11. Paul gives thanks to the Father who has qualified believers 'to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light,' Colossians 1:12, and Peter speaks of an inheritance that is 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you,' 1 Peter 1:4. The correspondence is of a gift allotted by God, not earned. The type falls short in that the land of Canaan could be lost to foreign rulers, whereas the inheritance in Christ is kept safe.

study.christ:
Psalm 125 leads to Christ by promise, by pattern and by the sheer shape of its hope. The first promise is stability. A people who trust in the LORD are as immovable as Mount Zion, and the New Testament says that stability is found in a person. In Isaiah 28:16 God lays a stone in Zion and says that whoever believes will never be shaken. Peter reads that stone as Christ, and so does Paul, for believers are built 'on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone,' Ephesians 2:20. The security of the person who trusts is therefore a share in the security of the stone on which he rests. The writer to the Hebrews adds that 'we are receiving an unshakable kingdom,' Hebrews 12:28.

The second promise is the ring. 'As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds His people.' Jesus speaks of His sheep in language that matches the double hold of the psalm: 'No one can snatch them out of My hand,' and then 'No one can snatch them out of My Father's hand,' John 10:28 to 29. The shepherd's hand and the Father's hand are laid round the flock. This is not a new teaching but the psalm's picture made personal. Paul runs through every possible threat, trouble, distress, persecution, famine, danger and sword, and says that none of them can separate the believer from the love of Christ, Romans 8:35 to 39. The hills are replaced by the love of the One who died.

The third promise concerns the scepter. The wicked scepter that presses on the land is set against another. Psalm 45:6 says that 'justice is the scepter of Your kingdom,' and the writer to the Hebrews gives those words to the Son, Hebrews 1:8. Revelation pictures Him ruling with an iron scepter, Revelation 19:15. The psalm's prayer that the wicked scepter will not rest is answered by the One whose scepter is righteous and whose throne endures for ever. Jesus Himself lived under a foreign scepter in the land allotted to Israel, and He did not let it shape His hands. He did no injustice, and when He was struck He did not strike back. In that sense the prayer 'so that the righteous will not put forth their hands to injustice' was fully answered in the Righteous One.

The last verses speak of those who are good and those who turn to crooked ways, and the New Testament shows that only One is good in the full sense. The 'upright in heart' are those who have been made so in Him. When the psalm closes with 'Peace be upon Israel,' Paul takes up the benediction for the Israel of God, Galatians 6:16, and says that Christ 'Himself is our peace,' Ephesians 2:14.

Care is needed here. The psalm is not a veiled prophecy in every line, and the mountains round Jerusalem are not a code. The psalm speaks of a real city and a real land. The links to Christ are those the New Testament itself draws: the stone, the hand, the scepter, the inheritance and the peace. They are enough to show that what Israel asked of the LORD in this psalm is given in the person of His Son.
study.god:
The psalm shows a God who is both a foundation and a defender. The image of Zion that 'abides forever' makes the first point: He does not change, and those who rest on Him are not moved. Isaiah 26:4 speaks of 'GOD the LORD' as 'the Rock eternal,' and the psalm sets that rock under the feet of the people. His stability is shared. The trusting are 'like Mount Zion,' which means that His steadfastness is given to those who lean on Him.

He is a God who encircles. The repetition of 'around' tells us that His care is not at one point only but on every side. The prophets pictured Him as 'a wall of fire around' Jerusalem, Zechariah 2:5, and Psalm 34:7 says that the angel of the LORD 'encamps around those who fear Him.' There is no side of the believer's life from which God is absent. The phrase 'both now and forevermore' means this care does not lapse with the generations.

He is a God who governs history. The scepter of the wicked is real, but it is subject to the LORD's limit, and that is a claim about who is finally sovereign. Psalm 76:10 says that 'even the wrath of man shall praise You.' The wicked do not hold their power independently. God allows, bounds and ends it. The doctrine of providence is not a vague optimism here. It is a specific claim about boundaries set on tyranny, and it is made by a people who suffered from it.

He cares about the character of His people as well as their comfort. The purpose clause, 'so that the righteous will not put forth their hands to injustice,' shows that He is concerned that oppression does not turn the oppressed into oppressors. The prayer 'Do good, O LORD, to those who are good' assumes that He does good and that His goodness has a moral shape. God is not merely the protector of a nation. He is the judge of the heart.

He is also a God who judges. The crooked are led off with the evildoers, and the psalm does not apologise for that. His justice is the other side of His protection. Those who are secure inside the ring are secure because He keeps out what would destroy them, and the same God removes those who choose a twisted path.

For worship, the psalm teaches steady trust, not frantic activity. It invites a person to look at the horizon, remember who surrounds him, and wait. It asks for integrity and gives a benediction, 'Peace be upon Israel,' that blesses those who walk straight. The God of the psalm is a mountain and a wall, and He is also a judge and a giver of peace.

crossReferences.note: The pilgrim psalm of keeping closes, 'The LORD will watch over your coming and going both now and forevermore.' Psalm 125:2 uses the same phrase, 'both now and forevermore,' about the LORD surrounding His people. The two psalms together describe a keeper who watches and a ring that encloses.

God is within the city, 'she will not be moved,' and He helps her when morning dawns. It uses the same verb as Psalm 125:1 for being moved. Where Psalm 46 says that the city cannot be moved because God is in her, Psalm 125 says that the people who trust cannot be moved because He is round them.

The one who lives with integrity, who lends without interest and refuses a bribe against the innocent, 'will never be shaken.' The psalm sets security alongside moral character, as Psalm 125 does when it prays that the righteous not reach for injustice and that the LORD do good to the good.

The LORD promises to be 'a wall of fire around it' and 'the glory within it.' The picture is the same as Psalm 125:2, with the LORD as the encircling protection, and it adds that He is also at the center. He is both the ring and the glory inside it.

Elisha's servant is afraid of the army around the city. The LORD opens his eyes and he sees that the hills are full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha. It makes visible what Psalm 125 asserts about the LORD surrounding His people, and it shows that the ring is real even when unseen.

The tribal portions of the land were assigned by lot in the LORD's presence. The 'land allotted' in Psalm 125:3 recalls this. The land is a gift divided by God, and the psalm therefore speaks of an oppressor's scepter settling on ground that God Himself apportioned.

The prophet tells the people not to trust in deceptive words, chanting, 'This is the temple of the LORD.' The confidence of Psalm 125 is real but conditional on trust and uprightness. It guards against a reading that treats Zion as a talisman rather than as a place where the LORD is trusted.

God lays a tested stone in Zion, a sure foundation, and the one who believes will never be shaken. It explains the secret behind Psalm 125:1. The stability of Zion is the stability of what God has laid there, and the person who trusts shares it.

The wise builder's house stands on rock when the rain falls and the floods come. The psalm's immovable mountain becomes a house that survives the storm, and the condition is the same, that the person hears and acts on the words of Jesus. Trust and obedience belong together in both texts.

Jesus says that no one can snatch His sheep out of His hand or out of the Father's hand. The ring of mountains round Jerusalem becomes the double grasp of Son and Father. It is the psalm's promise of security spoken by the One who has the power to keep it.

Paul writes, 'Peace and mercy to all who walk by this rule, even to the Israel of God.' It echoes the close of Psalm 125, 'Peace be upon Israel,' and shows how the New Testament understands the blessing, as given to all who walk by the cross of Christ, Jew and Gentile alike.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a people placed in a land and a garden, under the rule of God, and the first thing the serpent tried was to move them off their trust. All of human history afterwards is a contest between two scepters, the rule of God and the rule of the wicked, and between two ways of living, the straight path and the crooked one. Psalm 125 lives at that fault line. It says that the people who trust in the LORD stand as firmly as a mountain, and that the wicked rule has a limit.

The psalm answers a question left by the earlier Psalter and by Israel's history. If God gave the land by lot to the tribes, how can foreign scepters lie over it? The answer is that they will not rest there for ever. The story of the judges, the kings and the exile shows how true that is and how costly. Israel was removed from the land when her own leaders turned to crooked ways, and the promises to the land were passed on to a coming king. The prophets said that a shoot would come from David's line and rule with justice, Isaiah 9:7.

The story reaches its centre in Christ, who lived under a foreign scepter in the allotted land and did not turn to injustice. He is the stone laid in Zion, the Shepherd who holds His sheep, and the King whose scepter is justice. At the cross the wicked scepter did its worst, and it did not rest. The tomb was empty and the kingdom was proclaimed. Through Him the promise to Israel is enlarged. Peace is on 'the Israel of God,' Galatians 6:16, a people drawn from every nation who trust in Him and are held in His hand.

Until the end, believers still live under the shadow of lesser scepters, and still need the prayer of verse 3 and the warning of verse 5. They live as pilgrims, with the mountains of God's care round them. The new creation is the full answer. 'We are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells,' 2 Peter 3:13. There the nations will no longer be ruled by the wicked, the people of God will not be tempted to compromise, and the city on the mountain will be unshakable. The Lamb stands on Mount Zion, Revelation 14:1, and the peace that the psalm sings, 'Peace be upon Israel,' becomes the settled condition of all who belong to Him.

sermon.title: Three Songs of Faith
sermon.why: Begg treats Psalms 123 to 125 together, showing how this psalm's picture of Zion's immovable stability grounds the pilgrim's confidence in the LORD's surrounding protection.

quiz.q: What are those who trust in the LORD compared to in verse 1?

options.text: Mount Zion, which cannot be moved and abides forever.
options.note: This is the psalm's central image of unshakeable stability.

options.text: A reed shaken by the wind.
options.note: This is the opposite image; the psalm stresses immovability, not fragility.

options.text: A ship tossed on stormy seas.
options.note: The psalm's picture is stability, not being tossed about.

options.text: A tent that can be quickly relocated.
options.note: Close to the theme of dwelling, but the specific image given is a fixed, immovable mountain.

quiz.q: How does verse 2 describe the LORD's protection of His people?

options.text: As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds His people.
options.note: This is the exact simile the psalm uses for the LORD's encompassing protection.

options.text: As a distant observer who rarely intervenes.
options.note: The psalm pictures constant, encompassing nearness, not distance.

options.text: As a single wall built on one side of the city.
options.note: The image is of surrounding mountains on every side, not one wall.

options.text: As a river that occasionally floods the land.
options.note: Rivers and floods appear in Psalm 124, not this psalm's protective imagery.

quiz.q: What does verse 3 say about the scepter of the wicked?

options.text: It will not rest permanently on the land allotted to the righteous.
options.note: This is the psalm's assurance that unjust rule over God's people has a limit.

options.text: It will rule forever without end.
options.note: The psalm promises the opposite, a limit on wicked rule.

options.text: It will be handed over willingly by the righteous.
options.note: The text speaks of God limiting the wicked's rule, not the righteous surrendering power.

options.text: It will only affect foreign nations, never Israel.
options.note: The verse specifically concerns the land allotted to the righteous, Israel's own territory.

quiz.q: What concern does verse 3 raise about prolonged wicked rule?

options.text: That the righteous might be provoked to stretch out their hands to do wrong.
options.note: This is the specific danger the psalm names, injustice tempting even the righteous to compromise.

options.text: That the righteous would become wealthy.
options.note: Wealth is not the concern raised; moral compromise under oppression is.

options.text: That the land would become physically barren.
options.note: The concern is moral and spiritual, not agricultural.

options.text: That foreign trade would decline.
options.note: Trade is not mentioned; the concern is the righteous being tempted toward wrongdoing.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament pick up this psalm's picture of unshakeable security?

options.text: Jesus promises that no one can snatch His sheep out of His hand.
options.note: John 10:28-29 gives the deeper fulfillment of the immovable security pictured in Mount Zion.

options.text: It teaches that believers can never feel secure in this life.
options.note: The New Testament offers strong assurance of security in Christ, the opposite of this claim.

options.text: It limits this security to angels alone.
options.note: John 10 explicitly applies this security to Christ's sheep, His people, not angels.

options.text: It replaces security with a call to relentless anxiety.
options.note: This misrepresents the New Testament's consistent call to confident trust in Christ's keeping.

questions: The psalm compares those who trust the LORD to an immovable mountain. Where in your life do you feel unstable, and how might deeper trust in the LORD steady you there?
The LORD surrounds His people the way mountains ring Jerusalem, on every side. Do you experience God's protection as all-encompassing, or only in certain areas of your life?
The psalm worries that prolonged injustice might provoke the righteous to compromise. Where are you tempted to do wrong because oppression or unfairness has gone on too long?
The psalm prays for good to come to the upright in heart. What would it look like for you to actively pray this blessing over fellow believers this week?
Jesus promises that no one can snatch His sheep from His hand. How does that promise change the way you face threats to your faith or your security?

translationNotes.note: Trust, batach, conveys confident reliance, not mere hope; it is the ground for the psalm's picture of Zion's immovable stability.
Scepter can also be rendered rod or staff, an image of ruling authority; its 'resting' pictures prolonged, settled occupation rather than a brief raid.
Peace be upon Israel closes the psalm with shalom, the same wholeness and security prayed for Jerusalem in Psalm 122:6-9.
